Correto. The cells in this image contain secretory granules that stain with either hematoxylin (magenta) or eosin (pink-orange), reflecting the chemical properties of the proteins they contain. The granules are distributed throughout the cytoplasm, indicating that these cells lack polarity, a feature commonly seen in endocrine cells. The pale-staining region adjacent to some of the nuclei indicates the presence of a large Golgi apparatus (“negative Golgi” image). Pituitary gland, 1000x

Correto. The staining properties of secretory granules depend on their contents. These secretory cells in a salivary gland contain basophilic secretory granules, indicating that their contents are negatively charged. Like the pancreas, these are enzyme-containing zymogen granules that will fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing their contents by exocytosis into the lumen of the acinus. Also visible are portions of the duct system that drains the gland. Submandibular gland, 1000x

Correto. These pancreatic cells are arranged in spheres called acini or alveoli and accumulate secretory granules in their apical regions; the base of each cell has abundant RER. The restricted apical distribution of the granules and the basally-located RER, is an example of cell polarity, a feature commonly seen in exocrine glands. The granules eventually fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing their contents by exocytosis into the lumen of the acinus. In this example, the secretory granules contain digestive enzymes and are referred to as zymogen granules. Exocrine pancreas, 1000x.
